::: {.chapter-subtitle}
A claim to test, not a creed to defend.

## Start with a headline you believe

Every spring, Indian newspapers carry a version of the same story. The monsoon will be weak this
year, the story says, because of El Nino. Farmers should expect a poor kharif season, food prices
will rise, and rural demand will soften. The story is not silly. It is written by competent
journalists from official forecasts, and most economists reading it would nod along.

Nod along, and then look at what the sentence actually did. The Pacific was warm. Warm Pacific
years are, on average, drier over India. A drier year means a smaller harvest. A smaller harvest
means higher prices and weaker demand. Each of those steps is a tendency, and the headline welded
four tendencies into a chain and then attached the word "because" to the front of it. Nothing in
the chain is a cause of anything in particular. It is a set of probabilities wearing the clothes of
an explanation.^[**Sources:** the structure of the seasonal forecast follows the India
Meteorological Department's long-period-average convention, in which a season below about 90 per
cent of the long-period average is classed as deficient, and the June-to-September monsoon supplies
roughly three-quarters of India's annual rainfall. **Read more:** the module's Topic 0 slides carry
the current year's figures, which change annually and are deliberately not printed here.]

Be precise about how loose the chain is, because the looseness is the lesson. The
correlation between El Nino and a weak Indian monsoon is real and it is physical, not a statistical
accident. It is also only about minus 0.5 to minus 0.6, and it weakened after the 1980s. In 1997
the Pacific ran one of the strongest El Ninos ever recorded and the monsoon was normal. A
relationship can be genuinely causal, well understood in its mechanism, and still fail to predict
any individual year. When that is true, it is not an explanation of any individual year either.

We will meet this problem in every chapter of this book, usually with worse data and higher stakes.
Did the monsoon fail and empty the cities of the Indus? Did a plague end the Roman peace? Did
climate cause the Bronze Age collapse? Students write those sentences confidently, and the sentences
have the same shape as the headline: a real physical relationship, a real historical event, and a
"because" inserted where the evidence supports only a "sometimes, on average".

So here is a case that runs the other way, and it is the best one in the book. Egypt kept a
continuous annual record of the Nile flood from 622 CE, because flood height set the land tax. The
two lowest floods in thirteen hundred years, in 967 and 1200, both coincide with famines, which is
what you would expect. Then comes the Fatimid famine of 1065 to 1072, the *shidda al-uzma*, the
great calamity, one of the worst subsistence crises in Egyptian history. The gauge says the water
was about half a standard deviation below normal. In other words, nearly fine. What produced the
famine was civil war, the collapse of the military, and the breakdown of the system that moved grain
from where it grew to where it was eaten. The harvest was not the binding problem. The entitlement
to the harvest was.^[**Sources:** the Roda Nilometer series, ed. Toussoun (1925), digitised by
Koutsoyiannis et al. (2013); on the Fatimid crisis and its non-climatic character, the discussion in
this book's Chapter 3. **Read more:** Koutsoyiannis (2013), doi:10.1080/02626667.2013.804626.]

Your intuition was reasonable. The evidence sometimes refuses it. The rest of this introduction is
the apparatus for telling those two situations apart.

## The view from the other shore

Imagine the world economy not from London or New York but from a beach on the Malabar coast, or the
deck of a dhow running before the monsoon from Aden to Gujarat. It is a deliberately awkward place
to stand, because almost every long-run history of the world economy is written from somewhere
else: from the North Atlantic, looking outward, with Europe as the active party and the rest of the
world as the stage on which European energy plays out. Tell the story that way and its shape is
settled before the evidence arrives. The world is poor and static until, around 1500 or 1750,
Europe stirs, and modern prosperity radiates from a single source.

Stand on the Indian Ocean shore instead and a different shape appears. For most of recorded history
the largest and richest economies, and the most commercially developed, were in Asia: Han and Song
China, the Abbasid caliphate, Mughal India. The world's most coveted store of value, silver and
gold, flowed toward them rather than away. Europe spent long centuries as a periphery, exporting
slaves, furs and raw metal, importing manufactures and ideas, and paying for what it wanted in
bullion it could barely produce itself. The period in which Europe genuinely ran the world economy
is short, concentrated in the century or so after 1750, and even at its height it rested on the
Asian periphery it governed.

The default reverses things more thoroughly than that summary suggests. In 1000 CE the
largest cities in the world were Baghdad, Kaifeng and Cordoba, and Cordoba is the only one most
European readers will place. The most sophisticated commercial instruments of the age, the
partnership contract, the bill of exchange, deposit banking, were being used across the Islamic
world and in Song China before they appeared in Italy. And the goods that Europeans crossed oceans
to obtain in the fifteenth century had been moving across the Indian Ocean for a thousand years in
ships that Europeans did not build, on routes they did not know, in a trade whose prices they did
not set.

This book takes that view seriously enough to build a whole history around it. But the vantage
point is a tool. It earns its place by making an anomaly visible, and it should be dropped the
moment it stops paying. The argument it generates is a claim, and the book's job is to
test that claim period by period against what the evidence will bear, and to be candid about where
the evidence is thin and where serious scholars disagree.

## What we mean by a world economy

We should say what the object is before spending eleven chapters locating its centre, and this is
harder than it sounds. Most books in this field use the term and never define it, which is
convenient, because every definition either excludes most of the period or admits almost everything.

The definition this book works to is deliberately modest. A world economy is a set of regions whose
production and prices respond to one another across distances that none of them controls. Not a
world market, which would require something close to a single price; not an empire, which is a
political object; and not merely contact, since a diplomatic gift or a shipwrecked sailor
establishes contact without establishing anything economic. The test is responsiveness at a
distance, and the crucial word is *respond*: what happens in one place has to alter what is
produced, or what things cost, somewhere far enough away that no single authority governs both
ends.

That definition is weak on institutions and strong on responsiveness, and it is weak on institutions
on purpose. The institutions change out of all recognition across five and a half thousand years,
from temple redistribution to chartered companies to container shipping, and a definition anchored
to any of them would exclude most of the period. Responsiveness is the one thing that can, in
principle, be measured at every point on the arc, even if the instrument for measuring it changes
completely. It also sets a bar the book has to clear in each period rather than assume, which is
why Chapter 1's verdict on the centre of gravity is *not applicable* rather than *no*. In the third
millennium BCE the question does not yet have a subject.

## The spine: the claim we are testing

Here is the argument in one paragraph. The rest of the book interrogates it.

> *Viewed from the Indian Ocean, the world economy spent most of its history centred on
> Asia --- visible in the direction bullion flowed and in where the world's goods were made.
> Integration advanced and retreated in waves shaped by climate, disease, technology and
> money, along a durable maritime channel and a periodically resurgent overland one. Europe's
> dominance was real and transformative but bounded --- concentrated in the century after
> 1750, built partly on the Asian centrality it overturned, and resting at its height on the
> Indian Ocean periphery it governed. Its timing and depth remain debated, and the East's
> aggregate return --- measurable but partial, achieved within a Western-built order --- is the
> long arc closing, not simply repeating.*

Call this the spine. It treats European dominance as an interruption rather than a destination, but
a bounded one, and four qualifications bound it. They recur throughout the book, so carry all
four:

1. the interruption was consequential, roughly two transformative centuries rather than a blip;
2. its timing and depth are genuinely open, and are argued over in @sec-ch07;
3. the eventual return east is partial, being aggregate weight rather than a restoration of
   per-capita parity; and
4. it is system-dependent, since the Asian re-rise happened inside a US-anchored order.

We do not settle the spine here. We assemble the tools to test it, and return to weigh it in the
[Conclusion](11-conclusion.qmd).

## The framework: what makes a place productive

Underneath the whole book sits one piece of economics, stated plainly here because every chapter
refers back to it. What a society can produce depends on four things: its useful
knowledge, its capital, its people, and its land. Written out, output is a function of technology,
capital, labour and nature:

$$Y = f(A, K, L, N)$$

This is a scaffold, not a model to be solved. Nobody in this book estimates it. Its job is to make
us ask, once per topic, which of the four inputs was doing the work and which one was in the way.

**A is technology and useful knowledge.** Not only machines: techniques, crops, navigation, the
ability to write a contract that a stranger will honour. Institutions live here too, entered as
productivity rather than as a separate category, which is a simplification some economists will
dislike and which keeps the framework to four terms.

**K is capital assets.** Ships, warehouses, irrigation works, tools, pack animals, stock in hand.
A produced thing, not consumed at once, yielding services through time. That is the whole of what K
means in this book, and keeping it that narrow is deliberate, because three different ideas get
folded into it constantly.

Money is a function. It is what an object or a claim *does*: quote a price, settle a debt, hold
value between now and later. Silver by weight does it. So do cowries, coins, banknotes and a bank
deposit.

Credit is a relationship. One party holds a claim, another carries the liability, and purchasing
power has moved across time. The obligation can be written in silver, in grain, in cattle or in
coin, and Mesopotamia was running interest-bearing debt around 3000 BCE, two and a half millennia
before anyone struck a coin.

Capital is neither. It is a thing somebody built and can now use.

Money can finance capital and credit can finance capital, and it is tempting to conclude that they
are therefore capital. They are not. A society cannot make more because the ship was paid for with
borrowed silver rather than saved silver. The ship is the capital.

Follow one lump of metal and the three come apart cleanly. Silver in the ore body is N. Refined and
cast into an ingot it is output, and wealth. Used to quote a price or settle an obligation it is
performing a monetary function. Promised across time it sits inside a credit relationship. Four
positions, one metal, and the metal never changed.

Which is why the tidy version has to be resisted. That version says bullion is a good first and
becomes money later, at some date, and it is wrong in a way worth naming: it makes a claim about
the calendar when the real claim is about function. Refined silver is always an economic good. In a
great many societies it is also, at the same time, doing monetary work. Coinage standardises a
monetary object and certifies its content. It does not invent money.

The categories overlap, and that is the point rather than a defect. A bank deposit is money and a
credit claim at once. Cattle are capital and a store of wealth. The question is never which box
something belongs in. It is which function it is performing, here, in this transaction.

None of which costs us the tracer. Silver remains the best single thing to follow across five and a
half thousand years, and @sec-ch08 is where the direction it runs in reverses. What changes there
is what the metal is doing, and who will honour a face value at the far end of a voyage. It is not
a date on which metal turned into capital.

**L is labour and people.** In this book that means migration, slavery and indenture at least as
often as it means population growth, because for most of the period the way to get more labour into
a place was to move it there, and frequently to move it by force.

**N is land, energy and resources.** Most courses drop N, or fold it into capital, on the reasonable
grounds that in a modern economy land is a small share of costs. Before fossil fuel it is not a
small share of anything. Energy came from land, as food for people and animals and as wood for
heat; materials came from land; and the binding constraint on almost every pre-modern economy was
how much land it could reach. Restoring N to the front rank is the single most consequential thing
this framework does.

N also has a second face, and the second face is where the economics gets interesting. There is N
as nature: soil, rainfall, ore bodies, disease environment, the physical world a society is handed.
And there is N as power: what happens when a resource is not merely scarce but *concentrated*, so
that whoever holds the place it comes from can charge for access. Banda nutmeg, Potosi silver,
Baltic ship timber, the Straits of Malacca, Suez, the coalfields. Once you see the second face, a
great deal of what looks like commercial history turns out to be a fight over N. The armed trading
companies of @sec-ch06 are the clearest case: they are not merchants who happened to carry cannon,
they are organisations built to hold chokepoints.^[**Sources:** the framework follows the module's
own governing-framework document; on chokepoints and armed trade, @sec-ch06. **Read more:**
Findlay and O'Rourke, *Power and Plenty* (2007), for the same argument made at book length.]

Two long-run patterns fall straight out of the four terms, which is the main reason for having
them.

The first is Malthus, restated. With N roughly fixed and A improving slowly, any gain in output
gets absorbed by more people rather than by richer people. That is not a claim about human nature;
it is arithmetic on a constrained input. It is why almost every flourishing economy in the first six
chapters of this book flourishes by getting bigger, and why reading that as rising living standards
is the commonest mistake a student makes here.

The second is the escape, around 1800, and it is the same sentence run backwards. A surges, because
useful knowledge becomes cumulative and fossil-fuelled, and simultaneously the N constraint relaxes,
because coal substitutes for land as a source of energy and colonial acreage substitutes for
domestic acreage as a source of food and fibre. Both terms move at once, and only then does A
finally outrun L. @sec-ch07 is that story, and the framework is why the chapter can treat coal and
colonies as two versions of the same relief rather than as two unrelated advantages.^[**Sources:**
Wrigley, *Energy and the English Industrial Revolution* (2010), on the organic-economy constraint;
Pomeranz, *The Great Divergence* (2000), on ghost acreage. **Read more:** @sec-ch07.]

One sentence ties the framework to everything else in the book, and it is the sentence to memorise
if you memorise one:

> **The production function tells you what a society could produce; demand decides whether it does;
> and control of N decides who keeps the gains.**

Three separate claims, and the second and third are the ones usually left out. Capacity is the
supply side, and it is what the function describes. Demand is whether that capacity is used at all,
which is not automatic: European households had to acquire a taste for cotton, sugar and tea before
Asian and Atlantic production had a market to grow into, and Chapter 2 contains the only
pre-modern evidence in this book that anyone actually *ate* the pepper they imported. And power is
who captures the output once it exists, which is where the bottleneck-holder, the armed company and
the colonial state come in. A history that runs only on capacity ends up explaining why Britain
could industrialise and never explaining why India, which could also have done, did not.

Demand deserves a further sentence, because it is the term this kind of history most often drops.
It is easy to write a story in which Asia could produce and Europe could not, and to stop there.
But production without a buyer is not economic activity, it is a warehouse.

Some of the largest movements in this book are movements in what people wanted rather than in what
could be made: the
European acquisition of a taste for sweetened tea, which reorganised agriculture on three
continents; the shift of pepper from a ritual and medical substance to a culinary one, which
changed the volume required without changing the supply chain at all; the Chinese demand for
silver as a tax medium, which is why American mines mattered to a country that never traded with
the Americas.

When a chapter cannot explain why a flow started, the missing term is usually this one.

In practice the framework is used one line at a time. At the end of every chapter there is an input
ledger: which of the four inputs was doing the work in this period, and which one was binding?

The answers are not always the ones you would guess. In @sec-ch01 the binding input is N, but not in
the way the phrase suggests, because the constraint on the Indus cities turns out to be the
*variability* of the water rather than its quantity. In @sec-ch06 the input that moves is K, since
what the chartered company supplies is not better technology or cheaper labour but a way of
assembling capital and violence in the same institution. By @sec-ch10 the binding input has become
A, and the argument about whether it will stay that way is the argument about the next fifty years.

Ten lines, one per chapter. By the end you will have written the book's argument yourselves.

## The four questions, and where they meet the framework

The book asks the same four questions of every period. They organise every chapter and they are the
method the book hands you.

::: {.callout-important}
## The four motivating questions
- **Q1 --- Direction.** Is the system integrating or disintegrating? Two refinements the evidence
  forces on the simple cycle: integration breeds fragility, since the links that carry goods carry
  shocks; and disintegration has winners, since a fracturing core can loosen its grip on a
  periphery.
- **Q2 --- Channels.** Which routes carry the integrating weight? Three run through this book: the
  maritime Indian Ocean, the desert-and-oasis corridor, and the steppe. The ocean is the durable
  artery; the overland channels had one true climax, the Mongol Pax of @sec-ch04.
- **Q3 --- Modes.** What crosses the connection? The answer is read off the framework, input by
  input. The real flows are output itself, useful knowledge, people and capital assets --- Y, A, L
  and K. Alongside them run monetary and financial flows: settlement assets, and claims and
  liabilities. Bullion can sit on both sides at once, which is why its direction serves as the
  book's running tracer of the centre of gravity.
- **Q4 --- Europe.** What is Europe's role: peripheral, entrant, dominant, one of several cores? And
  how does it change? Asked as an open question, not assumed.
:::

Q4 is the odd one out and readers are entitled to ask why Europe gets a question to itself. The
answer is not that Europe is more important than the other actors; for most of this book it is
plainly less so. It is that Europe is where the reader's prior sits. Every student arriving at this
module has absorbed a version of the story in which European development is the main sequence and
everything else is background. The way to test a prior is to make it a question rather than leave
it as an assumption.

So Q4 asks in each period what Europe's role actually was, with the
possible answers laid out in advance and none of them privileged: peripheral, entrant, one core
among several, dominant. Asked that way, the answer changes across the ten chapters in a pattern
that is genuinely interesting, and in @sec-ch01 it changes twice, since Bronze Age Europe turns out
to be a resource periphery supplying tin to an Asian-centred system, which is a much stranger
finding than either "central" or "absent".

The four questions and the production function are not two separate pieces of apparatus. They are
two axes of the same one. The production function is vertical: it asks what makes a *place*
productive. The four questions are horizontal: they ask how places *connect*. And they meet at N.

That gives us a definition of integration with some economics in it. To integrate is to relax your
own binding constraint by drawing on somebody else's inputs: importing land-intensive goods because
you have run out of land, monetising foreign silver because your own mines are poor, importing
labour because you cannot raise enough of it, borrowing technology because you did not invent it.
Q3's four flows are the four inputs. Goods are N embodied, in the sense that a cargo of grain or tin
is somebody else's land arriving in usable form. Technology is A. People are L. Capital is K. The
mapping is close enough to be useful and loose enough that you should check it in each period rather
than assume it.

## Where the centre of gravity sat, and how sure we are

The spine is a claim about where the weight of the world economy sat, and a claim like that is only
as good as its definition of weight.

**Weight is output.** The centre of gravity is the point world economic activity balances around,
and the quantity being balanced is production. Not territory, not armies, and not population for
its own sake.

**Not all output counts equally.** What the spine is about is the connected economy: output that
trade enabled, or that was produced for trade, and above all for long-distance trade. A subsistence
farmer's grain is output, and in aggregate it dwarfs everything else in every chapter before the
nineteenth century, but it never moved and it cannot move a centre of gravity. So the weighting
favours the goods that travelled, the workshops that made them and the ports that handled them.
This is why a chapter can call Rome the largest single economy of its age and still put the centre
of gravity east of it. The two statements measure different things and both are true.

That choice needs defending rather than asserting, because there is an obvious objection and it is
a good one. The connected economy was small: in the periods this book opens with, the long-distance
trade is on the order of a few per cent of the output of the economies doing it. Weight the small
connected part and disregard the enormous subsistence part, and you have built a measure that
locates the centre wherever the tradeable goods were made. Since the tradeable goods were largely
made in Asia, Asia cannot lose. A reader entitled to be suspicious will say the measure was chosen
to produce the answer.

The reply is that the two measures answer different questions, and this book is asking the second
one. Total output answers *where was most production happening*, which before 1800 is very nearly
*where did most people live*. That is a real fact and a large one, but it tells you nothing about
who could set a price. Connected output answers *whose goods did other people reorganise themselves
to obtain, and on whose terms*. That question has testable consequences, which is what makes it
worth asking: it predicts where metal accumulated, which is physically observable in hoards and ice
cores; and it predicts who could refuse a deal. Chapter 2 catches the second one happening, when
Indian merchants stopped accepting Roman silver at the moment its content fell.

Two honesties follow. For much of the arc the two measures agree, because population and production
moved together, so the choice is doing less work than the objection implies. But they come apart
exactly where the argument is most contested, and the book will say which one it is using at those
points. And the measure is not neutral about what counts as economic weight: it treats the ability
to set terms as the thing worth measuring. That is a position, and a reader who thinks aggregate
production is the better question will read the same evidence and reach a different verdict. They
are entitled to.

**Before about 1800, output is read through population**, and the circularity has to be said out
loud. In a Malthusian world more food meant more people rather than richer people, so a region's
share of world output tracked its share of world population fairly closely, which makes population
a defensible proxy. But most historical output estimates for the pre-modern world were themselves
built from population figures and assumed income levels. When the two series agree before 1800,
part of that agreement is a fact about the world and part of it is an artefact of how the numbers
were made. A good student will spot this, and it is much better coming from us.

**Bullion indicates; it does not define.** The direction metal flowed is this book's running tracer,
because metal moved toward the workshop. It is evidence for where the centre lay, and good
evidence. It is not what the centre *is*.

**Every verdict is scored, on a four-point scale plus a null.** *High* means several instruments
with different biases give one answer. *Moderate* means the reading is supported, but one
instrument is carrying it. *Low* means it is a reasonable reading and a different one would not be
unreasonable. And *not applicable* means the question has no meaning in this period yet, which is
an honest answer rather than a dodge, and is the entry for @sec-ch01.

**Direction and magnitude are scored separately**, because they are separate claims and the evidence
for them is usually of different quality. Chapter 2 is the standing example: that Roman metal moved
east is about as secure as anything in ancient economic history, and how much of it moved is
contested by two orders of magnitude. An answer that gives one confidence level for both has run
two claims together.

Applying that scale across all ten verdicts turns up something worth knowing before you start.
**This book knows direction far better than it knows magnitude.** Of the nine periods where the
question has a subject, seven score high on direction and five score low on scale. We can say with
some confidence which way the weight sat and which way it was moving, in almost every period. We
can rarely say by how much. That asymmetry is not a failing of this particular book; it is a
property of the evidence, since the instruments that establish direction, such as the way metal
flowed or what a place exported against what it imported, are robust to being wrong about
quantities by a factor of two. It does mean that a reader who wants numbers will be more often
disappointed than a reader who wants an argument, and it is why @sec-appC now scores the two
separately.

**Two instruments, not one.** For nine chapters the centre has to be inferred, from city sizes,
trade composition, the direction of bullion, shares of world manufacturing. In @sec-ch10 it can
also be computed: Danny Quah's economic centre of gravity, the distance-weighted average location
of world output. That calculation is offered there as a complement to the reading this book has
been making all along, not as a replacement. It weights all output equally, where this book weights
connected output, so it answers a slightly different question, and two differently-derived readings
that agree are worth more than either alone.

**One switch, announced in advance.** Chapters 1 to 6 score aggregate weight; from @sec-ch07 the
measure that matters becomes income per head. That switch *is* the Great Divergence, and the
chapter says so. But it does mean the early and late verdicts are not marks on
the same ruler, and @sec-appC keeps them in one table precisely so that the seam is visible.

### The bullion tracer, and why it flips

Before modern capital markets, metal moved toward the workshop. People who made things the rest of
the world wanted, Indian cotton and Chinese silk and porcelain, were paid in silver and gold, which
pooled where production was most valued. So in antiquity Roman silver drained east to India
(@sec-ch02), and in the early-modern centuries New World silver flowed east to China (@sec-ch05).
The tracer even works in reverse where it should: the Abbasid core paid silver north to its
slave-and-fur periphery (@sec-ch03), mirroring Rome. That reversal matters, because a tracer that
only ever points one way is a rule rather than an instrument.

One complication belongs here rather than in a footnote, because it arrives before the pattern
does. The earliest traceable silver flow in this book runs the wrong way. In the third and second
millennia BCE, the metal moves *west to east* into Mesopotamia rather than east toward a workshop,
because at that date the workshop in the later sense does not exist and silver is moving toward
demand rather than toward production. So the tracer that organises eight chapters is complicated by
the first one. That is not a reason to drop it. It is a reason to state what the tracer assumes: it
works when one region is making things another region wants badly enough to pay in metal for, and
before that condition holds, metal moves for other reasons entirely.

After the nineteenth century the tracer flips, and what flips is not the obvious thing.

The metal is doing something new. Under the classical gold standard, gold is not merely accepted by
weight at the far end of a voyage; it anchors a settlement system that reaches across borders, and
claims denominated in it circulate on the credit of institutions rather than on assay. Follow it
then and it leads to the financial core, London and afterwards New York, rather than to the
workshop.

Note who underwrote that core. India's colonial drain helped finance Britain's payments deficits
(@sec-ch08), sourced in the periphery and intermediated by the centre.

### Integration breeds fragility

Q1's first refinement earns a paragraph of its own, because it is the closest thing this book has
to a general finding. The links that carry goods carry shocks. A network that moves pepper
efficiently moves pathogens efficiently, and a system whose parts have specialised in what they do
best is a system in which no part can feed itself when the connections fail.

The pattern shows up at every scale. The Late Bronze Age palaces fell more or less together, and
the tin that made their bronze came from far enough away that a single interruption reached all of
them. The Antonine plague travelled the same routes as the eastern trade and struck both ends of
Eurasia within a few years. The Black Death moved along the Mongol roads that had just made
overland trade viable for the first time in centuries. The financial crisis of the 1930s
transmitted through exactly the capital-market linkages that had been the previous generation's
achievement.

The lesson is not that integration is bad, which would be a strange thing to conclude from a book
about it. It is that integration and fragility are the same property observed at different moments,
and that a period's prosperity and its vulnerability are usually built out of the same links. When
a chapter reports a system at its peak, the useful next question is what that peak has made it
unable to survive.

## The two yardsticks

The book measures two different things and keeps them apart, and half the disagreements in this
field are two people scoring on different instruments without noticing.

**Integration** is measured two ways, because the evidence changes. Before there are prices, it is
read from the diffusion of goods, weights and standards: Indus seals turning up in Mesopotamia,
a chariot design reaching Shang China. That establishes that two economies touched, and says
almost nothing about how much, how often, or at what price. Once there is coinage and quoted
prices, integration can be read from price convergence instead, which is a far stronger
instrument. Two instruments, one concept, and the switch happens around @sec-ch03.

**Success** is the other yardstick, and it has two settings. Quantity, or extensive growth, means
more people, bigger cities, larger total output: prosperity turned into numbers. Quality, or
intensive growth, means sustained income per head, which is the modern escape and, on this
timescale, a very recent one. Almost every thriving economy in this book is thriving on the first
setting. Han China, Song China, Mughal India, Qing China: all much larger than their contemporaries,
none of them richer per person in the way the phrase implies today.

So say which yardstick you are using. An answer that says China was richer than Europe in 1700
without saying whether it means in aggregate or per head has not yet said anything.

## Most of the economy was never priced

One more piece of arithmetic before the evidence, and it is the one most likely to be forgotten.
For almost all of the period this book covers, most of what was produced was never bought or sold.

Think of output as three layers. The bottom and by far the largest is subsistence and obligation:
what a household grew and ate, plus what it handed over as rent, tribute, tithe or labour dues.
That second category has no clean modern counterpart, and it matters, because a peasant handing
over a third of the harvest is transferring real output without any price being formed anywhere.
Above that sits regional exchange, in local markets, at prices that were real but seldom recorded.
Above that, thinnest of all, sits long-distance trade.

Our evidence comes overwhelmingly from the top layer, because that is the layer that generated
records: customs registers, merchant letters, tax farms, port dues. So when a source gives us a
number, the first question is always what the number is a number *of*. A figure for the value of
the eastern trade is not a figure for the Roman economy, and treating one as a share of the other
requires knowing how much of the economy was never in the accounts at all.

Confuse the layers and it goes badly. Chapter 2 has to ask how
large the Roman eastern trade was, and the published estimates of the annual value of Rome's Indian
Ocean imports run from about 920 million sesterces to about 17,640 million. The high end is roughly
the size of the most-cited estimate of the entire Roman economy. Nobody involved is careless: the
estimates differ because each takes the tax assessment of one documented cargo and multiplies it by
an assumed number of ships, and the assumptions differ. But notice what has happened. A number
drawn entirely from the thin top layer, the customs record, is being compared with a number for all
three layers at once, and the comparison only works if you know what fraction of Roman output ever
passed through a market at all. It did not, and we do not.

## Trade costs, and what price convergence cannot see

The strongest instrument in the book is price convergence, and what it does is narrower than its
reputation. The test is not that a good costs the same in two places, because it never does. The test is
that the gap between the two prices is bounded by the cost of moving the good, and narrows as that
cost falls. A stable price gap between two trading places is therefore not a market failing to
integrate. It is the cost of integration, quoted.

Put slightly more formally, trade settles where the gap the market will bear equals the trade cost:
freight, plus tolls, plus risk, plus whatever has to be paid for protection. That last term is why
integration in this book is as much a political variable as a technological one. And it means a
narrowing gap can arise three ways. Demand can rise where the good is bought; supply can rise where
it is sold; or the cost of carriage can fall. Only the third is integration. So the sentence to
carry into the exam is that rising volumes are not evidence of integration. Converging prices
are.^[**Sources:** Shiue and Keller, "Markets in China and Europe on the eve of the Industrial
Revolution", *American Economic Review* 97 (2007), for the method applied comparatively. **Read
more:** @sec-ch06 and @sec-ch08, where the test does most of its work.]

The instrument also has a blind spot worth knowing, because it is exactly the blind spot that
matters in the early chapters. A good arriving somewhere for the first time has no prior price to
converge on. A chariot reaching Shang China, or the potato reaching Ireland, is integration that
this test cannot see at all. Before roughly 500 BCE we are working almost entirely in the blind
spot, which is why @sec-ch01 has to lean on diffusion and says so.

@sec-ch01 does, though, contain one place where the test can almost be run, and it shows what the
instrument feels like when it works. In the Old Assyrian trade of the
early second millennium BCE, tin bought at Assur cost about 6.7 shekels of silver per hundred
shekels of tin, and the same tin sold in Anatolia at about 14.3. That is a gap of roughly 2.1 times
across about a thousand kilometres of donkey caravan. It is not arbitrage, because arbitrage is
riskless and simultaneous and this was neither: the merchant financed the goods, waited a hundred
days, and bore the risk of losing everything to bandits or a change of ruler. The gap is the cost
of carriage, quoted, in a world with no coinage and no market in the modern sense. And the gap did
not close. It persisted for generations, which tells you that the costs were structural rather than
a temporary friction somebody was about to compete away.

## The kinds of evidence this book is built from

Every period in this book is known through a different instrument, and the instrument decides what
can be claimed. A chapter resting on ice cores can say things a chapter resting on customs
registers cannot, and vice versa, and neither can say what a chapter resting on a national accounts
series can. Most of the mistakes students make in this field are not mistakes about history. They
are claims made at a level of precision the instrument does not support.

The production function gives that survey its shape, because each input has its own evidence base
and its own characteristic way of going wrong.

### N: land, climate and resources

The evidence for N is mostly physical and mostly not written by anybody. Ice cores from Greenland
and the Alps record atmospheric deposition year by year, so a layer of lead in the ice is a
by-product of somebody smelting silver out of galena a continent away. Speleothems, which is to say
stalagmites, record rainfall in their oxygen isotopes. Lake sediments, pollen cores, marine cores
off river deltas and tree rings all give climate at various resolutions. Ore bodies have chemical
fingerprints, so a metal object can sometimes be traced to the ground it came out of.

The characteristic failure is dating, and the second is scale. A stalagmite might be dated to
within a century, which sounds precise until you need to know whether a drought preceded a
civilisation's collapse or followed it. Chapter 1 contains the cleanest instance in the book: three
independent archives agree that the climate around 2200 BCE got drier, and their error bands are
each as wide as the three-century gap they are being asked to bridge, so none of them can order the
climate event against the settlement change it supposedly caused. Synchrony is not sequence, and
without sequence there is no causation. The scale problem is related. A core measures its own
catchment, not the world, and a Greenland record weighted toward north-west Europe should not be
read as a statement about global production.

### L: people

Population is reconstructed from settlement survey, from cemetery demography, from skeletal and
stature evidence, and increasingly from ancient DNA. Isotopes in tooth enamel give something
different again: strontium and oxygen laid down in childhood record where a person grew up, and
enamel never remodels, so the molars carry an ordered record of where somebody was at particular
ages.

The characteristic failure of population evidence is worth stating as a rule, because it recurs.
**Almost every population figure in this book is an area multiplied by an assumed number of people
per unit of area, and the assumed coefficient does most of the work.** Change the coefficient and
the answer changes proportionally; change your mind about which line on the ground counts as the
edge of the settlement and it changes by more than that. @sec-appD sets out two worked cases: an
urbanisation rate for Sumer where two careful scholars differ by a factor of three, and a
population for Pataliputra where the published estimates span a factor of about thirteen without
anybody disputing any evidence at all.

Isotopes and DNA look like two ways of measuring the same thing and are not. **Isotopes measure
residence; DNA measures descent.** A merchant who sailed to Carthage, traded for a season and
sailed home is visible to the first instrument and completely invisible to the second, because he
left no descendants there. His grandchild, born in Carthage to a local mother, is the exact
reverse. This is why the finding that western Mediterranean Punic populations carry almost no
Levantine ancestry shows that Phoenician settlers did not dominate the gene pool. It does not show
that Phoenicians did not go there.

Both instruments report lower bounds, and where they disagree the disagreement is itself a
measurement: it is the ratio of circulation to settlement, which is a real economic quantity and
one we would otherwise have no way to see. It also forces a correction on a sentence people say
loosely. Goods and techniques travelled further than *settlers*. Whether they travelled further
than *people* is a different claim, and usually not the one the evidence supports.^[**Sources:**
Ringbauer et al., "Punic people were genetically diverse with almost no Levantine ancestors",
*Nature* 643 (2025), 139-47, doi:10.1038/s41586-025-08913-3. **Read more:** @sec-ch02 and
@sec-ch03, where both instruments are used.]

### K: capital, money and credit

One heading covers three things the framework keeps apart, and the reason is the archives rather
than the economics. Hoards, stray finds, die studies and bullion shipment records are evidence
about money. Loan tablets and partnership contracts are evidence about credit. Ship timbers,
irrigation surveys and warehouse accounts are evidence about capital itself. In practice they
arrive in the same box, because the people who wrote down one of them wrote down the others on the
same tablet.

So the evidence for all three is hoards, stray coin finds, mint output estimated from die studies,
bullion shipment records where a state bothered to keep them, and above all merchant archives: the
letters, loans and accounts of people doing business. Keep the categories separate when reading
them. Coin tells you about settlement; it does not tell you how many ships there were.

Its characteristic failure is that archives survive by accident, and disproportionately by
catastrophe. Mesopotamia's cuneiform tablets were unbaked clay, and what fired them hard enough to
last four thousand years was the burning of the palaces that held them. We read those economies in
detail because they were destroyed. A place that was never sacked, or whose records were kept on
palm leaf or paper in a wet climate, is not less commercial. It is less legible. Coin hoards carry
their own version of the same problem: a hoard dates when somebody decided to bury money and did
not come back for it, which is a fact about insecurity as much as about circulation, and which can
post-date the arrival of the coins by a generation.

There is a second and subtler difficulty with monetary evidence, which is that coins are recycled.
The metal in a coin struck in 200 CE may have been mined in 50 BCE, melted down twice and alloyed
with something else on the way. So a chemical analysis of coinage tells you what was in the melting
pot, not what came out of the ground, and the two questions have different answers. Chapter 2 puts
an ice core and a coin series side by side for exactly this reason: the ice records what was
smelted, and the coins record what was refined and recycled. They look like two measurements of one
thing and they are not.

### A: technology and technique

A is read from the objects themselves, and from the sciences that interrogate them:
archaeometallurgy, lead and tin isotope provenancing, residue analysis, and radiocarbon dating of
the contexts things are found in.

Its characteristic failure runs the opposite way to the others, and it is a cheerful one. **Better
dating destroys more claims than it creates.** When a technique improves, the usual result is that
something long believed turns out to rest on a specimen that is intrusive, or younger than its
context, or misidentified. Chapter 1 carries the cleanest example: domestic chickens were for
decades said to originate in the Indus Valley, and a systematic re-dating programme found that
every European Neolithic and Bronze Age specimen tested was intrusive, moving the earliest secure
domestic chickens to Thailand and about a thousand years later. Nothing was fabricated and nobody
was careless. The instrument got sharper and a claim fell over.

That is worth holding onto as a disposition rather than a fact, because it tells you how to read
the confident sentences in older books, including good ones. A claim about origins that was
established before radiocarbon calibration, or before isotope provenancing, or before it was
possible to sequence a genome from a tooth, has not been refuted. It has simply never been tested
by the instrument that could test it. Some of those claims will survive. The pattern of the last
twenty years is that most do not.

### What each proxy can and cannot support

Set the limits out in one place, because most over-claiming in this field is one of these four
moves.

| Proxy | What it supports | What it does not |
|---|---|---|
| Diffusion of goods | Contact, and the geographic range of a network | Volume, frequency, price, or who profited |
| Direction of carriage | Relative shipping cost; which end wanted the other's goods | How the surplus was divided between the two ends |
| Population | Aggregate scale, under a Malthusian assumption | Income per head, ever |
| Settlement counts | An upper bound on decline | The decline itself, since the record-keeping collapses too |

: What the standard proxies will and will not bear. {tbl-colwidths="[22,40,38]"}

The fourth row is the subtlest and the most often missed. When a state falls apart, the number of
attested settlements drops. But the thing that produced the attestations, an administration writing
things down, fell apart at the same time. So a fall in recorded settlements is a composite of real
decline and lost visibility, and it gives you a ceiling on the first rather than a measurement of
it.

### Absence of data is not absence of activity

What survives reflects record-keeping conventions and the accidents of climate and preservation,
not economic weight. Organic records rot in the humid monsoon tropics and survive in cool dry
Europe and arid Egypt, so the surviving record systematically under-documents the ocean world this
book is written around.

Because the direction of that bias is known, it licenses exactly one move: treat every figure we
have as a lower bound. That is a real licence and a useful one. It supports claims about direction
and it supports the statement that a trade was at least as large as the record shows.

It licenses nothing else, and in particular it does not license filling the gap with a conclusion.
A student who writes "the evidence is biased against Asia, therefore Asian trade was much larger"
has done exactly what the monsoon headline did: taken a real tendency and converted it into a
specific claim the tendency cannot carry. The bias tells you which way to lean. It does not tell
you how far.

### The evidence map is the inverse of the production map

One commodity demonstrates the whole problem, and it is the commodity this book returns to most
often. Black pepper is south Indian, and every Roman-period peppercorn ever recovered survives in
one of exactly three ways. Desiccated, in the hyper-arid Egyptian desert at Berenike and Myos
Hormos. Waterlogged, in anaerobic mud in Germany, Britain and France. Or mineralised, chemically
replaced in cesspit fill in Campania. Too dry for microbes, too wet for oxygen, or turned to stone.

The monsoon Indian Ocean littoral, where the pepper was actually grown, offers none of the three.
Warm, wet and oxygenated is the worst possible combination for preservation. So the finds are
thousands of peppercorns from Egypt, dozens from north-west Europe, and until very recently
essentially none from the producing region. Read that distribution as a trade map and you would
conclude that pepper was an Egyptian and European commodity.

The transferable version is this: the map of the evidence is not the map of the economy, it is the
map of the preservation conditions. Ask yourself which commodities have no preservation window
anywhere, and the answer, uncomfortably, is textiles. Cotton and silk rot in every climate that
grew them.^[**Sources:** Cobb, on the recovery contexts of Roman-period pepper, citing Cappers
(2006), Livarda (2011), and Robinson and Rowan (2015). **Read more:** @sec-ch02.]

There is a second version of the same problem, and it operates at a scale that is hard to take in.
When the ice sheets melted the sea rose roughly 120 metres, and it drowned the continental shelves.
Sundaland, the shelf joining Borneo, Java and Sumatra to mainland Asia, was about 4.7 million square
kilometres of dry land at the last glacial maximum against about 2.3 million today. Something on
the order of two and a third million square kilometres went under water. That is an area about the
size of India, and it went under along exactly the kind of coastline where people prefer to live.

Now ask what has been recovered from it. From the whole submerged Sunda shelf the record is some
six thousand vertebrate fossils and two fragments of *Homo erectus* skull, dated to around 140,000
years ago. No artefacts. No structures. No settlements. And even that material was not found by
archaeologists: it came up in a commercial dredging operation that removed five million cubic metres
of sand to build an artificial island.

This one cuts in a direction students find uncomfortable, so be exact. It does not
show that there were drowned cities, and people who want there to have been drowned cities reach
for it constantly. It shows something more disciplined and more useful: that an area the size of
India has been removed from the evidence base along the most habitable margin of a densely peopled
part of the world, and that on that shelf almost nobody has looked. The honest statement is not that there was
more down there. It is that for this region in this period the record is not thin because the
activity was thin. It is thin because the ground is under a hundred metres of water.

That is the pepper argument again in a different medium, and it is the strongest version of it in
the book. Which is exactly why it is the one most often over-driven, and why the closing of the
argument is the part to watch. The closing is more interesting than the opening.

Europe is the control case, because there people have looked. A four-year European research network
assembled a register of submerged prehistoric finds that now holds about 2,640 records, and the
shape of that register is the answer. Around 58 per cent are single finds rather than sites. Only
about one in six is an undisturbed occupation layer. Depth is recorded for under a third, and of
those nearly nine in ten lie shallower than five metres, with three sites in all of Europe recorded
deeper than forty. Denmark alone accounts for two-thirds of the total, which is a fact about Danish
research funding rather than about Danish prehistory. And the volume reporting all this says plainly
that evidence for settlement or in-situ activity from waters more than twelve nautical miles
offshore has yet to be found in the North Sea, or anywhere else in the world.

So the submerged record is real, and substantial, and shallow, fragmentary and forager-shaped.
There is no gradient in it pointing toward greater complexity further out.

Keep the positive case in view, though, because otherwise this reads as an argument that nothing
can be found under water. Things can. Atlit-Yam, off the Carmel coast in Israel, is a
Neolithic village of about nine thousand years ago sitting four hundred metres offshore under eight
to twelve metres of water: stone-built structures, burials, and a stone-lined well nearly six metres
deep. It is one of more than twenty submerged prehistoric sites known off that one coastline. That
is what a drowned settlement looks like when it survives and somebody excavates it, and the thing to
notice is how ordinary it is. Its economy is continuous with its contemporaries on land.

Say why the deeper water stays unlooked-at, because the reason is economic rather than
intellectual. A single exploratory survey with ship time runs to two or three million dollars,
and anything systematic is an order of magnitude more. So the work that does happen is usually
piggy-backed on something commercial. When a sonar survey for the Qatar-Bahrain causeway threw up
83 features of possible archaeological interest, divers inspected about half of them, and every one
turned out to be modern or natural. That is the honest state of the question: not a search that has
failed, and not a search that has succeeded, but a search that has barely been funded.

The chronology closes the question from the other end. Sea level came within about a metre of its
present position by roughly five thousand years ago. Uruk reached 250 hectares, and writing
appeared, at about 3100 BCE. Before that, Mesopotamian villages were rarely larger than one or two
hectares. The shelves therefore finished drowning before the first city existed anywhere, and the
whole window during which they flooded runs, in the words of the field's own flagship volume, from
mobile hunter-gatherers with no pottery, no agriculture and no metal tools at one end to small towns
at the other. Both ends of that window are on dry land, in the record, where we can see them.

Which gives the general form of the move, and you will need it more than once. A preservation gap
licenses "we cannot see what was there". It never licenses "what was there was X". Getting to X
needs positive evidence, and where X is a civilisation the positive evidence is not confined to the
drowned strip: cities need quarries, farmland, hinterlands, refuse and trade goods, none of which
stops politely at the old shoreline. The step from "we cannot see" to "therefore something
particular was there" is the step this section exists to refuse.^[**Sources:** Bailey, Galanidou,
Peeters, Jons and Mennenga (eds), *The Archaeology of Europe's Drowned Landscapes* (Springer, 2020),
open access, for the site register, its composition and the offshore-settlement statement; Ur,
"Households and the emergence of cities in ancient Mesopotamia", *Cambridge Archaeological Journal*
24 (2014), 249-68, for Uruk and the Ubaid village sizes. **Read more:** Bailey and Flemming,
*Quaternary Science Reviews* 27 (2008), 2153-65, which is the founding statement of the
preservation-bias argument and is also, usefully, sceptical about over-reading it.]^[**Sources:** on the land areas, Sathiamurthy and Voris, "Maps of Holocene sea level
transgression and submerged lakes on the Sunda Shelf", *Natural History Journal of Chulalongkorn
University* Suppl. 2 (2006), Table 1; on the hominin material, Berghuis et al., "The late Middle
Pleistocene *Homo erectus* of the Madura Strait, first hominin fossils from submerged Sundaland",
*Quaternary Environments and Humans* 3 (2025), 100068, doi:10.1016/j.qeh.2025.100068. **Read more:**
Hanebuth, Stattegger and Grootes, *Science* 288 (2000), 1033-35, on how fast the shelf drowned.]

### The oldest annual series in the world are tax records

The longest continuous annual measurements we have of anything physical were not made by anybody
interested in the physical world. The Nile flood runs annually from 622 CE because flood height set
the Egyptian land tax. The Beaune grape harvest runs from 1354 because the town council had to pay
the pickers on a date. Lake Suwa's freeze runs from 1443 because a shrine read the ice for an omen.

Nobody was measuring the climate. They were measuring a tax base, a wage bill, an omen and a
season, and climate is the by-product. Which means the geography of the pre-modern climate record
is a map of fiscal and institutional capacity, and it degrades when the polity degrades. The
Nilometer holds between seventy-seven and a hundred readings per century up to 1470, and then
thirty-two in the sixteenth century and thirty-one in the seventeenth. The density of a series is
itself a datum about the state that produced it.

Two cautions on that particular series, since it recurs in this book. The apparent upward drift
after about 1300 is the river bed silting up and raising the gauge datum, not a wetter Nile. And
only the annual maximum is the tax-relevant variable, so it is the only one that was recorded with
consistent care.^[**Sources:** Toussoun (1925), digitised by Koutsoyiannis et al. (2013); Kondrashov,
Feliks and Ghil (2005) on the series' spectral structure. **Read more:** @sec-ch03.]

### Claims carry grades, and a passed check is not a verified fact

Because the evidence is so uneven, this book grades individual claims as well as verdicts. A claim
is **secure** when a named source has been read and says it. It is **probable** when it takes one
step of inference, or rests on a synthesis rather than the original study. It is **contested** when
specialists disagree in print, in which case the disagreement is taught rather than resolved away.
And it is **single-source** when one authority stands behind it and nobody has independently
confirmed it, which is a warning rather than a criticism.

One exercise shows what that grading finds. In preparing @sec-ch02 this
book compiled a register of claims about early historic South Asia. On the forty-five entries whose
subject is genuinely South Asian, fifteen and a half per cent came out secure and twenty-nine per
cent contested. Fewer than one claim in six about the Mauryan and post-Mauryan economy is secure on
the book's own grading. That ratio is itself a finding, and a more useful one than most of the
individual claims, because it tells you how to read every confident sentence written about the
period, including the ones in this book.

A recent case shows what the grading is for, and it is still live. In
2023 a team published a study of Gunung Padang in West Java arguing that the hill is not a hill but
a construction, begun between 25,000 and 14,000 BCE, and "potentially the oldest pyramid in the
world". The journal retracted it in March 2024, and the reason given is this section's whole
argument in one sentence: the radiocarbon dating "was applied to soil samples that were not
associated with any artifacts or features that could be reliably interpreted as anthropogenic".

Notice what is and is not wrong there. The dates are probably fine and the laboratory work looks
careful. What failed is the join between the number and the claim. The age belongs to the soil; the
construction event was inferred separately, from geophysics, and then had the soil's age attached
to it. Ask of any number in this book what it is a number *of*, and you will catch that class of
error before it catches you. The authors still disagree with the retraction, so the case is
still open.^[**Sources:** Natawidjaja et al., "Geo-archaeological
prospecting of Gunung Padang buried prehistoric pyramid in West Java, Indonesia", *Archaeological
Prospection* 31:2, doi:10.1002/arp.1912, retracted at doi:10.1002/arp.1932 on 18 March 2024.
**Read more:** Ernenwein, "Retraction and reflection", *ArcheoSciences* 49-1 (2025), 607-10, the
editor's own account of the case.]

There is a last rule, and it is the one that cost this book the most to learn. **A passed check is
not a verified fact.** An earlier version of Chapter 1 was fact-checked, and the check certified as
correct a claim about the Uluburun shipwreck's cargo that was false. It passed because the check
compared the chapter against the documents then to hand, and the claim had been *inherited* from
one of them rather than tested against the wreck's excavation report. Agreement between two
documents that share an ancestor is not evidence. It is an echo. When you are checking a number,
the question is never whether it matches what else you have read. It is whether anybody ever
measured it.

### The instruments improve, and that is itself the shape of the book

Set the four evidence bases against the chapters and a progression appears which is worth stating
once, because it governs what each half of the book is able to argue.

For @sec-ch01 there are no prices at all. Not few: none. Integration has to be read from the
diffusion of objects and standards, and the verdict on the centre of gravity is therefore *not
applicable*. From @sec-ch02 there are coins, quoted prices in a handful of documents, and the first
physical output series, so direction can be argued and magnitude cannot. From @sec-ch03 to
@sec-ch06 the merchant archives thicken and price series begin to run continuously in a few places,
which is enough to test convergence over decades. From @sec-ch07 there are wages, prices and the
first constructed national accounts, and the argument shifts from where the weight sat to why it
moved. By @sec-ch09 and @sec-ch10 there are trade statistics collected by states for their own
purposes, and finally a centre of gravity that can be computed rather than inferred.

Two things follow. The first is that the book's later verdicts are better evidenced than its
earlier ones, which is simply true and is stated in @sec-appC chapter by chapter. The second is the
one people forget: better evidence does not make the later arguments less contested. @sec-ch07 has
more data behind it than any chapter before it and contains the book's least settled question. The
quantity of evidence and the level of disagreement are close to independent of one another, and
assuming otherwise is how a reader ends up trusting a well-measured claim more than it deserves.

## One cargo, and what four questions can do with it

It helps to see the apparatus run once on a real object before the chapters start, and there is a
good one to hand. In the late fourteenth century BCE a ship went down off Uluburun, near Kas on the
southern Turkish coast, and it was found in 1982. It is the richest single deposit of Bronze Age
trade goods ever recovered, and it is a dataset of one.

What was aboard: about ten tonnes of copper, as 354 four-cornered "oxhide" ingots and 121
bun-shaped ones, and roughly a tonne of tin. That is close to the ten-to-one ratio bronze needs, so
the cargo is about eleven tonnes of alloy in kit form. Also about 175 glass ingots, around a tonne
of terebinth resin in at least 149 Canaanite jars, 135 Cypriot vessels, African ebony, hippopotamus
and elephant ivory, Baltic amber and Mesopotamian bitumen. Products of at least nine or ten
cultures, in one hull.

Now run the questions. **Q2, channels**, it answers well: this is a maritime cargo moving
counter-clockwise around the eastern Mediterranean, and the amber alone establishes a link running
to the Baltic. **Q3, modes**, it answers partly: the flow here is overwhelmingly goods, which is N
embodied, and the presence of merchants' pan-balance weight sets on the Syrian shekel of about 9.3
grams suggests private commercial calculation rather than pure gift exchange. **Q1, direction**, it
barely touches, because one wreck is a point and direction requires a series. And **Q4, Europe**,
it raises without settling, because where the tin came from is precisely what two laboratories now
disagree about.

Then ask what it cannot tell you, which is the more useful half. It cannot tell you how many such
ships sailed, or how often, or what any of it cost, or who profited. It cannot even settle whether
this was commerce or diplomacy: royal shipments in the Amarna letters run to a hundred or two
hundred talents of copper, and 354 oxhide ingots is about 325 talents, which is the same order of
magnitude. And there is a preservation trap sitting inside it. The 135 Cypriot vessels aboard are
roughly twice the number known from the whole Aegean for the entire Late Bronze Age. If one wreck
can double the record, then the record was never a sample of the trade. It is a sample of what
happened not to be lost.^[**Sources:** Pulak, "The Uluburun shipwreck: an overview", *International
Journal of Nautical Archaeology* 27 (1998), 188-224, at p. 219 for the cultures represented and
p. 204 for the Cypriot vessels; on the dating, Pulak's own later statement of the end of the
fourteenth century and Manning et al. (2009) at 1320 plus or minus 15. **Read more:** @sec-ch01.]

## Three ledgers to keep

Ten topics can be ten surveys or one argument, and the difference is whether you write things down
as you go. Keep three running lists, one line per chapter.

The **centre-of-gravity ledger**: where is the weight, is it moving, and how confident are we, on
the four-point scale above. The **input ledger**: which of A, K, L and N is doing the work, and
which is binding. And the **natural-system beat**: the climate, energy or disease force in play,
which is there to stop the physical world becoming background scenery.

Three short rows a week. By @sec-ch10 you will have assembled the book's argument in your own
handwriting, which is a considerably better position to argue with it from than having read it.

## Six threads that run the length of the book

Six themes recur. Name them, because each one is a way of noticing something a straight chronology
would hide.

1. **Centre of gravity.** The spine itself, with an explicit verdict and a stated confidence in
   every chapter, collected in @sec-appC.
2. **Measurement of success: quantity to quality.** The correction described above, set up in
   @sec-ch01, running through the silver story in @sec-ch05 and @sec-ch06, and resolving at
   @sec-ch07 where the Great Divergence *is* the switch.
3. **Follow the silver.** The early-modern form of the bullion tracer. The same American silver met
   different monetary conditions and had different fates: Asia absorbed and specialised, the
   Ottomans inflated, West Africa debased and depleted, and Europe converted a monetary loss into
   armed-trade and financial power. That last fate is the bridge to the divergence.
4. **Measurement of integration.** The instruments improve over time, from diffusion, to bullion
   flows, to wages and prices, to national accounts, to a computed centre of gravity. Before prices
   only the first exists, which limits what @sec-ch01 and @sec-ch02 can claim.
5. **Forces.** Four drivers sit behind Q1's direction: climate, disease, technology and policy. Two
   of them are natural, which is a standing reminder that the world economy has always been
   embedded in a physical system rather than floating above one.
6. **Data survival and bias.** Everything in the previous section, carried forward as a habit.
   Whose eyes we are seeing through is itself a running question.

### The economy sits inside a physical system

Two of the four forces behind Q1 are natural, and that follows from the framework rather than
sitting beside it. If N is a first-class input, then climate, energy and disease are
not context. They enter the production function directly, as the quantity and reliability of what
the land yields and as the number of people available to work it.

This cuts both ways, and the second way is the one that needs guarding. It licenses taking physical
shocks seriously as economic events: a volcanic eruption that lowers a Nile flood is a fiscal
event, and a pandemic that removes a third of a labour force is a change in L with a century of
consequences. But it does not license reading every economic change as a physical one. The test
that keeps the two apart is simple and it is the most portable instrument in this book.
**Geography explains levels; only things that vary can explain timing.** A mountain range or a
prevailing wind can tell you why a place was persistently rich or persistently isolated. It can
never tell you why something happened in one century rather than another, because it did not
change. Climate, by contrast, does vary, which is exactly what makes it admissible where geography
is not, and exactly why it has to be dated precisely enough to bear the weight.

## A note on method

Two commitments follow, and they are why the subtitle is *data and debates*.

- **Data.** The book leans on numbers, because numbers are how you adjudicate a claim like the spine
  rather than assert it. Figures and tables are reproducible, generated from datasets you can
  download and re-run. But the data thin out sharply as you go back, and they are biased toward the
  literate, fiscal, European end of the record. A chapter on the Bronze Age and a chapter on the
  twentieth century are not equally evidenced, and the book says which is which.
- **Debates.** Where the scholarship is genuinely contested, and the standing examples are when the
  Great Divergence began and why, whether interwar disintegration was man-made or inevitable, and
  when globalisation really started, the book presents the disagreement rather than resolving it
  out of sight. Disputed figures are flagged and taught, not silently settled.

Be honest, too, about where this book stands in its own field, because the complaint it is built
on is not its invention. David Northrup observes that textbooks "almost invariably"
break their coverage at 1500, and Merry Wiesner-Hanks, introducing the *Cambridge World History*,
names the problem in her own preface while conceding that four of that series' nine books are given
to 1400 and after. Northrup pushes further back than 1500, and in a form that reaches this book's
own starting line: the deeper exclusion is the convention of beginning with Sumer and with writing,
which removes something between ninety-five and ninety-nine per cent of the human past before the
story starts.

There are honest defences of that imbalance and readers should have them. David Christian argues
the demographic case, that perhaps eighty per cent of all human lives were lived between the
Palaeolithic and 1750, which is a real argument for weighting the deep past. The counter is that
evidence, not lives, is what a historian can work with, and evidence accumulates toward the
present. And one chapter in the same volume goes after this book's method rather than its coverage:
Michael Lang argues that periodising by chronology, which is exactly what the ten chapters ahead
do, smuggles in assumptions about what changes and when. That objection is not answered here. It is
worth carrying while you read.^[**Sources:** Northrup, "Globalization in historical perspective", in
*The Cambridge World History*, vol. 1 (2015), pp. 110-31, at pp. 111-12 and 123; Wiesner-Hanks,
preface to vol. 1, pp. xvii and xix; Christian, "Introduction: the constructions of a global past",
vol. 1, pp. 22-23; Lang, "Evolution, rupture, and periodization", vol. 1, pp. 84-109, at pp. 96-97.
**Read more:** Sachsenmaier, "The evolution of world histories", vol. 1, pp. 56-83.]

One last thing, and it is what the subtitle is for. This book states a claim and then spends ten
chapters testing it, which means it is possible to read the evidence assembled here and reach a
different verdict. That is the intended use. The places where you are
most likely to end up disagreeing are marked: the chapters that rest on a single instrument, the
verdicts scored low on scale, the disputes set out in @sec-appE, and the derivations in @sec-appD
where a headline figure turns out to be a coefficient multiplied by an area. If you finish the book
convinced that European dominance was longer, or deeper, or earlier than the spine allows, the
useful question is which of those places you would have to attack to make that case. A claim you
cannot say how to falsify is a creed, and the point of setting the argument out this explicitly is
that this one is not.

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read the chapters
Each chapter opens by following one object that carries its period's story, locates the period on
the arc, sets out the cast and how we know, narrates the period on its own terms, then reads it
through the four questions, delivers a centre-of-gravity verdict with a confidence level, and hands
off to the next. Look out for the recurring Data exhibit and Debate, and the Follow the money and
How we know callouts. Three appendices do the heavy lifting the chapters send out to them:
@sec-appC collects the ten verdicts in one table, @sec-appD sets out how the most quotable numbers
were actually constructed, and @sec-appE gives the live scholarly disputes in full.
:::
